A 65-year-old Caucasian man visits the nephrology outpatient clinic for a follow-up appointment. He was previously diagnosed with stage G3a chronic kidney disease (CKD) and albuminuria stage A2. He follows strict dietary recommendations and takes enalapril. He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia which has been complicated by urinary tract obstruction. His vitals are stable, and his blood pressure is within the recommended limits. His most recent laboratory studies are as follows:
Serum sodium 140 mEq/L
Serum potassium 5.8 mEq/L
Serum chloride 102 mEq/L
Serum phosphate 4.0 mg/dL
Hemoglobin 11.5 mg/dL
Albumin excretion rate (AER) 280 mg/day
Which of the following is the best strategy in the management of this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 65-year-old Caucasian man visits the nephrology outpatient clinic for a follow-up appointment. He was previously diagnosed with stage G3a chronic kidney disease (CKD) and albuminuria stage A2. He follows strict dietary recommendations and takes enalapril. He has a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia which has been complicated by urinary tract obstruction. His vitals are stable, and his blood pressure is within the recommended limits. His most recent laboratory studies are as follows:
Serum sodium 140 mEq/L
Serum potassium 5.8 mEq/L
Serum chloride 102 mEq/L
Serum phosphate 4.0 mg/dL
Hemoglobin 11.5 mg/dL
Albumin excretion rate (AER) 280 mg/day
Which of the following is the best strategy in the management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Removal of enalapril
opb. Addition of furosemide
opc. Observation
opd. Addition of patiromer
ope. Addition of sevelamer

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient has stage G3a CKD and elevated serum potassium at 5.8 mEq/L, indicating hyperkalemia, which is a significant concern in CKD patients. Enalapril, an ACE inhibitor, can contribute to increased potassium levels, so its removal is a reasonable consideration. However, the addition of patiromer, a potassium binder, is a more direct and effective strategy for managing hyperkalemia. Furosemide can also help lower potassium levels but is less specific than patiromer for this purpose. Observation is not appropriate given the elevated potassium. Sevelamer is primarily used for phosphate control and is less urgent than addressing hyperkalemia. Therefore, the best management strategy is the addition of patiromer to effectively lower potassium levels and manage hyperkalemia.
